slides: Let's continue, with two tools that help in every motion question.

slides.say: Many motion questions have two travelers, or one trip in two parts. We organize them in a table.
The table has three columns, speed, distance and time. The distance goes in the middle, because the distance is the speed times the time.

slides: It's like the work table, team, work and time. Each traveler, or each part of the trip, gets its own row.
Now a new example. A cyclist rides two hours at fifteen kilometers per hour.

slides.say: That's part one. The speed is fifteen, and the time is two hours.
The distance is the speed times the time. Fifteen times two is thirty kilometers.
Then she rides twenty kilometers at ten kilometers per hour. That's part two.
The time is the distance divided by the speed. Twenty divided by ten is two hours.
So in every row, the distance is the speed times the time. When we know two boxes, the row gives us the third.

slides: Now the whole trip. We add a total row.

slides.say: The distances add up. Thirty plus twenty is fifty kilometers.
The times add up too. Two plus two is four hours.
But the speeds don't add up. Fifteen plus ten is not her speed on the whole trip. We'll see why in the next lesson, average speed.
Then we look for the link the question gives us. Equal times, equal distances, or a total.
at: Equal times, equal distances, or a total

slides.say: For example, if two travelers ride for the same time, we write their two times as equal. That gives us the equation.
And in every motion question, draw a sketch. It takes a few seconds, and it shows what really happens.
Draw the road, and mark where it starts and ends.
at: mark where it starts and ends

slides.say: Put a dot for each traveler, and write the time each one starts.
at: Put a dot for each traveler

slides.say: Draw an arrow for each direction, and write the speed on it.
at: Draw an arrow for each direction

slides.say: Mark the distance between them. That's the gap.
And when they meet, mark the meeting point. We'll solve questions like this one in the relative speed lesson.
Sometimes the directions are not on one line. A plane climbs at an angle. Or one person walks north, and another walks west.
Then the sketch is a right triangle.
at: Then the sketch is a right triangle

slides.say: The height and the ground are the two short sides. The path along the slope is the long side.
Remember Pythagoras, from topic thirty-one. We call the two short sides a and b, and the long side c. Then a squared plus b squared is equal to c squared.
at: Then a squared plus b squared

slides.say: For example, short sides three and four. Three squared is nine, and four squared is sixteen. Nine plus sixteen is twenty-five, and twenty-five is five squared. So the long side is five.

slides: So when the directions are different, always draw. And the distance in the formula is the real path, along the slope.

slides.say: So let's sum it up. Distance is equal to speed times time. In the triangle, cover the one you want.
at: Distance is equal to speed times time

slides.say: The units must match, and minutes become parts of an hour.
To change the units of a speed, use identical ratios. Change the time, and the distance in the same way.
at: To change the units of a speed

slides.say: Two travelers, or two parts? Make a table. Add the distances and the times, but never the speeds.
And always draw a sketch.
Take a moment to memorize this. Now try the first question, and I'll see you in the next video.
